content: Every day, both children and adults succumb to acute community-acquired bacterial meningitis, particularly in low-income countries. Survivors of this condition often face long-term complications such as deafness, epilepsy, and other neurological disabilities. Osmotic therapies, which are thought to draw fluid from the extravascular space and reduce cerebral edema, have been proposed as a potential adjunct to antibiotics to improve survival and neurological outcomes. This review is an update of a Cochrane Review first published in 2013. The objective of this review was to assess the effects of adding osmotic therapies to antibiotics in the treatment of acute bacterial meningitis in both children and adults, specifically focusing on outcomes such as mortality, deafness, and neurological disability. The search strategy included a comprehensive review of multiple databases, including CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, CINAHL, LILACS, and clinical trial registries, up to February 2017. Conference abstracts were also reviewed, and researchers in the field were contacted for additional data. The inclusion criteria were randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that evaluated any osmotic therapy in adults or children with acute bacterial meningitis. Two independent reviewers screened the search results and selected trials for inclusion. Data were analyzed using risk ratios (RR) and 95% confidence intervals (CI), with results stratified based on whether participants received steroids. The GRADE approach was used to assess the certainty of the evidence. Five trials involving a total of 1,451 participants were included in the review. Four trials compared glycerol to placebo, while one trial compared glycerol to 50% dextrose. Additionally, three trials included dexamethasone, and one trial included acetaminophen (paracetamol) in a factorial design. Stratified analyses showed no significant interaction between the use of steroids and the effects of glycerol. Aggregate effect estimates were presented. When compared to placebo, glycerol likely has little to no effect on mortality in individuals with bacterial meningitis (RR 1.08, 95% CI 0.90 to 1.30; 5 studies, 1,272 participants; moderate-certainty evidence). However, glycerol may reduce the risk of neurological disability (RR 0.73, 95% CI 0.53 to 1.00; 5 studies, 1,270 participants; low-certainty evidence). Glycerol may have little to no effect on the occurrence of seizures during meningitis treatment (RR 1.08, 95% CI 0.90 to 1.30; 4 studies, 1,090 participants; low-certainty evidence). It may also reduce the risk of subsequent deafness (RR 0.64, 95% CI 0.44 to 0.93; 5 studies, 922 participants; low to moderate-certainty evidence). Glycerol likely has little to no effect on the risk of gastrointestinal bleeding (RR 0.93, 95% CI 0.39 to 2.19; 3 studies, 607 participants; moderate-certainty evidence). The evidence regarding nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea is highly uncertain (RR 1.09, 95% CI 0.81 to 1.47; 2 studies, 851 participants; very low-certainty evidence). In conclusion, glycerol was the only osmotic therapy evaluated in these trials. The available data do not demonstrate a significant effect of glycerol on mortality. However, glycerol may reduce the risk of neurological disability and deafness in individuals with acute bacterial meningitis.
